problem.title: Mitigating 40K/s TCP TIME_WAIT Ephemeral Port Exhaustion in API Gateways

spark.summary: Resolve a 35% EADDRNOTAVAIL / 502 Bad Gateway outage on a 40,000 req/s API gateway caused by unpooled upstream TCP sockets exhausting all 28,232 Linux ephemeral ports in 60s TIME_WAIT.
spark.keyTakeaway: Switch to a 256-socket HTTP Keep-Alive / HTTP/2 upstream pool, widen ip_local_port_range to 1024..65535, enable tcp_tw_reuse=1, and add multi-IP SNAT diversity.
spark.byteSummary:
In Production Scenario #29, an NGINX/Envoy API gateway handling 40,000 outbound req/s suffered 35% `EADDRNOTAVAIL` failures and 502 Bad Gateways while host CPU sat at just 30%. Inspection via `ss -s` showed 28,232 sockets pinned in `TIME_WAIT`—exhausting the entire default `32768..60999` ephemeral port pool.

The root cause was misconfigured upstream proxying (missing `proxy_http_version 1.1` / `Connection ""`), forcing the gateway to open and close a fresh TCP socket per request and capping throughput at `28,232 / 60 = 470 req/s` per upstream tuple.

Remediation restores persistent HTTP Keep-Alive pooling (reducing open sockets to ~256), widens `ip_local_port_range` to `1024..65535`, enables `tcp_tw_reuse=1` with timestamps, and adds multi-IP SNAT + `TCP_tw` alerting to sustain 40,000+ req/s with zero 502s.

learningJourney.title: Stage 1: Incident Triage — 35% EADDRNOTAVAIL at 30% CPU
learningJourney.purpose: Diagnose ephemeral port exhaustion using ss -s, netstat, and gateway error logs.
learningJourney.explanation: When a gateway logs `connect() failed (99: Cannot assign requested address)` (`EADDRNOTAVAIL`) while CPU is 30%, run `ss -s` and `ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l`. Seeing ~28,232 `TIME_WAIT` sockets targeting the same upstream VIP confirms ephemeral port exhaustion.

sectionDiagram.title: Identifying a 28,232-Socket TIME_WAIT Storm at 30% CPU

cards.label: Check Inside Pod Netns
cards.detail: In Kubernetes, run ss -s inside the gateway pod's network namespace rather than the host node.

cards.label: Check Conntrack Too
cards.detail: Verify dmesg for 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet' if NAT/kube-proxy is in the path.

sectionDiagram.summary: 35% EADDRNOTAVAIL at 30% CPU with ~28,232 TIME_WAIT sockets in ss -s confirms unpooled outbound port exhaustion.
sectionDiagram.caption: 502 EADDRNOTAVAIL errors at 30% CPU with 28,232 TIME_WAIT sockets in ss -s pinpoint unpooled HTTP churn.

learningJourney.title: Stage 2: Fixing NGINX / Envoy Upstream Keep-Alive Pools
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate per-request socket teardown by enabling HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive or HTTP/2 upstream pools.
learningJourney.explanation: In NGINX, setting `upstream { keepalive 256; }` alone STILL closes connections unless `proxy_http_version 1.1;` and `proxy_set_header Connection "";` are configured (since HTTP/1.0 defaults to `Connection: close`). Enabling Keep-Alive reduces 40,000 req/s from 40,000 new sockets/sec down to 256 persistent reused sockets.

sectionDiagram.title: Fixing HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive Headers & Upstream Pool Sizing

cards.label: HTTP/2 Multiplexing
cards.detail: Upgrading upstream links to HTTP/2 or gRPC multiplexes hundreds of concurrent requests per TCP socket.

cards.label: Keepalive_requests Cap
cards.detail: Rotating a pooled socket every 10,000 requests balances load across newly scaled upstream pods.

sectionDiagram.summary: Enabling HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive headers and a 256-socket pool cuts 40K/s socket churn to near zero.
sectionDiagram.caption: Fixing proxy_http_version 1.1 and keepalive 256 sustains 40K req/s over 256 persistent sockets.

learningJourney.title: Stage 3: Sysctl Hardening (Port Range & tcp_tw_reuse)
learningJourney.purpose: Configure kernel sysctls safely for bursty fallback traffic and Kubernetes pod namespaces.
learningJourney.explanation: Apply `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 1024 65535` (64,511 ports), `net.ipv4.tcp_timestamps = 1`, and `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1` via DaemonSet or pod `securityContext.sysctls` (for safe namespaced sysctls). Also set `ip_local_reserved_ports` for any daemon listen ports in the 1024..65535 range.

sectionDiagram.title: Pod-Safe Sysctl Hardening for 64,511 Ephemeral Ports

cards.label: 2.3x Burst Runway
cards.detail: 64,511 ports sustain ~1,075 unpooled req/s per tuple during fallback bursts.

cards.label: No Root-Only Unsafe Flags
cards.detail: ip_local_port_range is a namespaced sysctl allowed in Kubernetes pods once whitelisted on kubelet.

sectionDiagram.summary: Widening ip_local_port_range with reserved listen ports and tcp_tw_reuse=1 adds safe kernel headroom in pod namespaces.
sectionDiagram.caption: Pod-namespaced sysctls widen ip_local_port_range to 1024..65535, reserve listen ports, and enable tcp_tw_reuse=1.

learningJourney.title: Stage 4: Multi-IP SNAT Pool for > 64K Concurrent Connections
learningJourney.purpose: Scale beyond 64,511 sockets to a single upstream VIP using multiple source IPs.
learningJourney.explanation: If long-lived WebSocket/SSE fan-out requires 200,000 concurrent connections to one upstream VIP, a single `src_ip` hits the 64,511-port ceiling. Attaching 4 secondary SNAT IPs (`M = 4`) expands unique 4-tuples to `4 * 64,511 = 258,044` sockets, using round-robin source IP selection.

sectionDiagram.title: Scaling Past 64K Concurrent Sockets via 4-IP SNAT Diversity

cards.label: 25% Safety Headroom
cards.detail: Provisioning 4 IPs for 200K connections leaves 22% headroom for rolling restarts and uneven hashing.

cards.label: Multiple Upstream VIPs
cards.detail: Alternatively, resolving 4 upstream pod IPs directly (headless service) multiplies 4-tuples without extra SNAT IPs.

sectionDiagram.summary: Multi-IP SNAT pools (or direct pod-IP load balancing) multiply 4-tuple capacity past 64,511 sockets per gateway.
sectionDiagram.caption: 4 SNAT source IPs paired with IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT expand capacity to 258K concurrent sockets.

learningJourney.title: Stage 5: Conntrack Table Sizing & Bypass for High-Churn Nodes
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent nf_conntrack table exhaustion when gateway pods sit behind Linux iptables/IPVS NAT.
learningJourney.explanation: Every TCP connection (including `TIME_WAIT` entries held for `nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait = 120s`) consumes ~320 bytes in `nf_conntrack`. Scaling `nf_conntrack_max` to `1,048,576` (with `hashsize = max / 4`) or enabling eBPF/Cilium DSR or `NOTRACK` on high-rate internal VIPs prevents silent conntrack packet drops.

sectionDiagram.title: Preventing Silent nf_conntrack Table Drops on NAT Nodes

cards.label: Silent Drop Hazard
cards.detail: When nf_conntrack fills, Linux drops new SYN packets silently—looking like mysterious 1s-3s TCP retransmit stalls.

cards.label: 320 MB for 1M Entries
cards.detail: Raising nf_conntrack_max to 1M costs only ~320 MB of kernel slab memory.

sectionDiagram.summary: Sizing nf_conntrack_max=1M with matching hashsize or using eBPF bypass prevents silent NAT packet drops.
sectionDiagram.caption: Raising nf_conntrack_max to 1M (hashsize=262K) or bypassing via eBPF prevents silent NAT SYN drops.

learningJourney.title: Stage 6: Graceful Draining & Avoiding Keep-Alive Race EOFs
learningJourney.purpose: Coordinate upstream pod shutdowns and idle timeouts so pooled sockets never hit stale 502s.
learningJourney.explanation: When an upstream pod scales down or closes an idle Keep-Alive socket at the exact millisecond the gateway writes a new request onto it, the gateway receives an `RST`/EOF and returns HTTP 502. Setting gateway `keepalive_timeout` (55s) < upstream `keepalive_timeout` (65s) and enabling idempotent-only retry on `GET`/`HEAD` eliminates race 502s.

sectionDiagram.title: Eliminating Stale-Socket 502s with Asymmetric Timeouts & Safe Retries

cards.label: 10-Second Timeout Gap
cards.detail: A 10s gap (55s client vs 65s server) prevents simultaneous close/write race conditions.

cards.label: Never Retry Non-Idempotent POSTs
cards.detail: Only retry a broken Keep-Alive socket on POST if 0 bytes were written or an Idempotency-Key is present.

sectionDiagram.summary: Asymmetric idle timeouts (55s < 65s), graceful Connection: close draining, and safe EOF retries eliminate Keep-Alive 502s.
sectionDiagram.caption: 55s gateway vs 65s upstream idle timeouts, graceful draining, and safe EOF retries prevent Keep-Alive race 502s.

learningJourney.title: Stage 7: Load-Test Verification & Continuous Port SLOs
learningJourney.purpose: Validate 40K+ req/s stability in staging and alert on TIME_WAIT regressions in production.
learningJourney.explanation: Before shipping, run a 10-minute 40K req/s soak test while asserting `ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l < 500`, zero `EADDRNOTAVAIL`, and `< 1%` new-connections-per-request ratio. In production, alert when `TCP_tw / ip_local_port_range > 0.60` or `TCPTimeWaitOverflow > 0`.

sectionDiagram.title: 40K Req/Sec Soak Verification & Production Port-Churn Alerts

cards.label: Regression Detection
cards.detail: A single NGINX config refactor dropping proxy_http_version 1.1 spikes new_conns/RPS to 100% immediately in staging.

cards.label: Zero 502s at 40K+ RPS
cards.detail: Persistent pooling + tuned sysctls keep open sockets < 500 and eliminate EADDRNOTAVAIL.

sectionDiagram.summary: 40K req/s soak assertions (TIME_WAIT < 500) and >60% port-range alerts prevent Keep-Alive regressions from reaching production.
sectionDiagram.caption: 40K req/s soak checks and node_sockstat_TCP_tw alerts verify < 500 open sockets and zero EADDRNOTAVAIL.

knowledgeChecks.question: You added `keepalive 256;` to an NGINX `upstream` block, but `ss -s` still shows 28,000 `TIME_WAIT` sockets and `EADDRNOTAVAIL` errors. Why?

options.text: NGINX defaults to HTTP/1.0 (`Connection: close`) to upstreams unless `proxy_http_version 1.1;` and `proxy_set_header Connection "";` are also set.
options.feedback: Correct. Without HTTP/1.1 and clearing the Connection header, NGINX closes every upstream socket after 1 request.

options.text: Because `keepalive 256;` only works for UDP traffic.
options.feedback: Incorrect. NGINX upstream keepalive is specifically for TCP/HTTP connections.

options.text: Because Linux forbids Keep-Alive on port 8080.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Keep-Alive works on any TCP port.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: NGINX proxy_pass uses HTTP/1.0 by default, which sends Connection: close unless proxy_http_version 1.1 and empty Connection header are set.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should the gateway's Keep-Alive idle timeout (55s) be set slightly SHORTER than the upstream server's Keep-Alive timeout (65s)?

options.text: So the gateway closes idle sockets cleanly on its own schedule rather than racing with an upstream close and hitting EOF/502.
options.feedback: Correct. Asymmetric timeouts prevent the gateway from writing a request onto a socket the upstream just closed.

options.text: To force the upstream server to enter `TIME_WAIT` instead of the gateway.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Only idle sockets (after 55s) are closed, which is negligible churn.
Incorrect. Idle timeouts do not disable conntrack.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Making client idle timeout < server idle timeout avoids close/write race conditions that cause sporadic 502s.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens if `nf_conntrack` fills up on a Kubernetes NAT node during a `TIME_WAIT` storm?

options.text: Linux silently drops new incoming/outbound SYN packets, causing 1s-3s TCP retransmit stalls or timeouts.
options.feedback: Correct. Raising nf_conntrack_max (or using eBPF/NOTRACK) prevents silent conntrack drops.
Incorrect. Kernel sysctls do not auto-scale on conntrack exhaustion.
Incorrect. TCP never falls back to UDP.

options.text: All existing Keep-Alive sockets gain 2x bandwidth.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Conntrack exhaustion drops new connections.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: A full nf_conntrack table drops new SYNs silently, requiring higher nf_conntrack_max or eBPF bypass.

beginner.summary: Fix 502 Bad Gateway port-exhaustion errors by turning on HTTP Keep-Alive connection pooling so the gateway reuses 256 sockets instead of opening new ones.
beginner.keyTakeaway: Reusing persistent connections drops open sockets from 28,232 in `TIME_WAIT` to under 500.
beginner.byteSummary:
If an API gateway opens a new TCP connection for every request, it runs out of ports at 470 req/s and returns 502 errors.

Turning on HTTP Keep-Alive connection pooling lets 40,000+ req/s share 256 open sockets.

intermediate.summary: Fix NGINX/Envoy Keep-Alive headers (`proxy_http_version 1.1`), widen `ip_local_port_range` to `1024..65535`, and enable `tcp_tw_reuse=1` in pod namespaces.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: 256-socket Keep-Alive pooling + 64,511 ephemeral ports + `tcp_tw_reuse=1` eliminates `EADDRNOTAVAIL` at 40K+ req/s.
intermediate.byteSummary:
Production Scenario #29's 35% `EADDRNOTAVAIL` failure was caused by missing HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive headers pinning 28,232 ports in 60s `TIME_WAIT`.

Enabling 256-socket Keep-Alive pooling, widening `ip_local_port_range` to `1024..65535`, and setting `tcp_tw_reuse=1` eliminates port exhaustion.

advanced.summary: Scale >64K concurrent sockets with multi-IP SNAT + `IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT`, size `nf_conntrack_max=1M`, align 55s<65s idle timeouts, and alert on `TCP_tw`.
advanced.keyTakeaway: Asymmetric idle timeouts (55s < 65s) prevent Keep-Alive race 502s, while `nf_conntrack_max=1M` and `TCP_tw` alerts protect NAT nodes.
advanced.byteSummary:
For >64K concurrent sockets to one VIP, use 4-IP SNAT + `IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT` and size `nf_conntrack_max=1M` (`hashsize=262K`) to prevent silent SYN drops.

Keep gateway idle timeout (55s) below upstream (65s), run 40K/s soak checks (`TIME_WAIT < 500`), and alert at 60% `TCP_tw`.

_nextProblem.title: Multi-Leader Conflicts: Beyond Last-Write-Wins
_nextProblem.prompt: Your active-active multi-region platform runs 3 regional leaders (US-East, EU-West, AP-South) handling 15,000 writes/sec for user shopping carts, feature toggles, and inventory counters. Asynchronous cross-region replication resolves concurrent updates via Last-Write-Wins (LWW) using `System.currentTimeMillis()`. Because of a +180 ms NTP drift on an EU-West node, an EU write occurring 100 ms *after* (or *before*) a US-East write carries a higher timestamp and silently overwrites newer US-East updates—losing ~0.4% of concurrent updates (60 lost updates/sec) with zero error logs. Redesign the conflict-resolution protocol.
